h1: How to Build a Restaurant Text List That Fills Tables on Slow Nights
metaTitle: Restaurant SMS Text Message Marketing (Fill Slow Nights)
metaDescription: A plain, click-by-click guide to restaurant SMS text message marketing. Build a permission-based text list that fills tables on slow nights.
heroAlt: A guest reading a restaurant text message offer on their phone
directAnswer: A restaurant text list is simply the phone numbers of guests who gave you permission to text them offers. To build one that fills slow nights, collect numbers the honest way (a sign-up keyword, table tents, a QR code at checkout), pick a simple texting tool, and send a short, specific deal a few hours before your slow night. Keep it to two to four texts a month, always with an easy opt-out. That warm list beats email or social for filling tables tonight.

intro:
It is 6:30 on a Tuesday in Brickell. Your kitchen is staffed, your food is ready, and half your tables are empty. You know there are people three blocks away who love your place. They just forgot you exist tonight. An Instagram post might reach a fraction of them tomorrow. You need them tonight.

There is one tool that lands in a pocket in seconds and gets read almost every time: a text message. Not a random blast to strangers, which is both illegal and a waste of money. A text to people who already ate with you and said, yes, text me your deals. That group is called your text list, and it is the single best way to fill tables on a slow night.

This guide shows you how to build that list from zero and use it without annoying anyone or breaking any rules. We will go click by click: how to collect numbers the right way, how to pick a simple texting tool, exactly what to send, and how to tell if it is working.

sections.h2: Why does a text beat email or social on a slow night?
sections.html:
First, a quick definition. SMS text message marketing just means sending a short text (SMS stands for Short Message Service, the plain texts your phone already sends) to guests who asked to hear from you. No app to download, no algorithm deciding who sees it. It goes straight to the phone in their pocket.

Here is why that matters on a slow night. An Instagram post reaches maybe a small slice of your followers, and only whenever they happen to open the app. An email often sits unopened for a day or lands in a promotions folder. A text gets looked at within minutes almost every time. When you need tables filled tonight, minutes matter.

There is a second reason, and it is bigger. Your social media following is rented, not owned. Instagram and Facebook decide who sees your posts, and they can change that overnight. Your text list is yours. Nobody can throttle it or charge you to reach your own guests. Every phone number you collect is an asset you keep.

None of this means you drop email or social. Those still do real work, and our slow-night playbook walks through using all of them together. But if you only have time to build one thing this month, build the text list. On a dead Tuesday, a single message to people who already love your food will do more than anything else you own.

sections.h2: The one rule you cannot skip: permission and an easy way out
sections.html:
Before you collect a single number, understand the one rule that keeps you safe and keeps guests happy. It is really the same rule twice: only text people who clearly said yes, and always give them an easy way to stop. In the United States a law called the TCPA (the Telephone Consumer Protection Act) governs marketing texts. You do not need to memorize it. You need three plain habits.

  1. Get real permission first (this is called an opt-in). Before you send any promotional text, the person must clearly agree to receive them. A box they check themselves on a sign-up form, a keyword they text you on purpose, or a paper sign-up under a line that says By joining you agree to get occasional texts all count. You cannot pre-check the box for them, and you cannot require it just to buy a meal.
  2. Always offer an easy opt-out. Every marketing text should tell people how to leave, usually the line Reply STOP to opt out. If someone replies STOP, the texts must end right away. Since 2025 you also have to honor an opt-out when a guest asks any reasonable way (in person, by email, over the phone), so tell your staff: if a regular says stop texting me, take them off the list.
  3. Never buy, rent, or scrape a list of numbers. Lists of phone numbers for sale are not people who agreed to hear from you. Texting them is against the law, and it is the fastest way to get your number blocked and pile up fines. The only good list is one you built yourself, one yes at a time.

One more piece of housekeeping that is new but easy. Since 2025, US phone carriers require any business texting from a regular 10-digit number to register it first (the industry calls this A2P 10DLC registration). It sounds technical, but in practice your texting tool walks you through a short form at setup. You confirm your business name and address, pay a small one-time fee (often just a few dollars), and you are done in a few days. Until it is registered, carriers may block your texts, so do not skip the setup steps your tool asks for.

That is the whole legal part, and it is not scary. It comes down to good manners: only text people who invited you, and let them leave whenever they want. Do that and you will never have a problem.

sections.h2: How do you collect phone numbers the right way?
sections.html:
You build a text list the same way you build regulars: a little at a time, at the moments guests are already happy. Here are five ways to collect numbers with permission built in. You do not need all five. Pick two and start this week.

1. Set up a text-in keyword

A keyword is a simple word people text to a number to join your list. You have seen it before: Text TACOS to 55555 for our specials. When they text that word, your tool automatically replies to confirm and adds them, with the opt-in handled for you.

  1. Inside your texting tool (we pick one in the next section), look for a menu item called Keywords or Grow your list.
  2. Create a keyword that fits your place, like BRICKELL or your restaurant name. Keep it short and easy to spell.
  3. Write the automatic welcome reply it sends back, for example: Welcome to [Restaurant]! You will get a few deals a month. Reply STOP to opt out.
  4. Save it, then put that keyword everywhere: table tents, the menu, your window, your Instagram bio.

2. Put a table tent on every table

A table tent is the little folded card that stands on the table. Print one that says Slow-night deals, straight to your phone. Text BRICKELL to 55555. Add the small print: A few texts a month, reply STOP anytime. Guests sitting with a phone already in hand are your easiest sign-ups.

3. Ask at the checkout or the register

The moment someone pays a bill they enjoyed is a great time to ask. Train your team to say one line: Want our slow-night specials by text? Just text this word. If you use a modern point-of-sale (the tablet or system you ring people up on, like Square, Toast, or Clover), it may offer to collect a phone number at checkout with an opt-in checkbox. Turn that feature on.

4. Use your guest Wi-Fi sign-in

If you offer guest Wi-Fi, you can ask for a phone number and a text opt-in on the login screen before people connect. Many Wi-Fi systems built for restaurants do this. It is a fair trade: free Wi-Fi for permission to text a few deals. Just make sure the opt-in is a clear checkbox, not automatic.

5. Add a QR code to receipts and the door

A QR code is the square barcode people scan with their phone camera to open a link. Your texting tool can create one that opens a join form. Print it on receipts, tape it by the door, or add it to your takeout bags. In a takeout-heavy neighborhood like Doral or Hialeah, the bag sticker alone can grow your list fast.

Whichever ones you choose, always show the honest small print (how many texts, and reply STOP to leave). It builds trust, and it keeps you on the right side of the rule from the last section.

sections.h2: How do you pick a texting tool without overthinking it?
sections.html:
A texting tool (also called an SMS platform) is just software that sends one text to your whole list at once, tracks who opted in, and handles the STOP replies for you. You do not text guests from your personal phone. You would lose track of who said yes, and one phone cannot send hundreds of messages cleanly. The good news: picking one is easier than it looks. There are two simple paths.

Path A: use what your point-of-sale already offers

If you ring up guests on Square, Toast, Clover, or SpotOn, marketing texts are very likely built in or a cheap add-on. This is the easiest path because your customer list and opt-ins already live there.

  1. Log in to your point-of-sale dashboard on a computer.
  2. Look in the menu for a tab called Marketing, Campaigns, or Loyalty.
  3. Find the Text or SMS option and click to turn it on. It will walk you through the one-time carrier registration we mentioned earlier.

Path B: use a standalone texting tool

If your register does not do texts, or you want more control, sign up for a dedicated tool. Well-known ones for small businesses include SimpleTexting, Textedly, and EZ Texting. They all do the same core job, so do not agonize over the choice.

  1. On a computer, go to the tool's website and click Sign up or Start free trial.
  2. Create your account with your business email.
  3. Follow the setup steps to get your texting number and complete the carrier registration form. Have your business name, address, and EIN (your business tax ID number) handy.
  4. Import your opted-in contacts, or start collecting them with the methods above.

On cost, plans are usually priced by how many texts you send. As a rough guide (prices change, so treat these as approximate), entry plans for a small restaurant often run about 25 to 50 dollars a month for a few hundred to a couple thousand texts, which is plenty when you are only messaging two to four times a month. Per-text overage is usually just a few cents. Do not buy a giant plan on day one. Start small, and grow the plan only when your list grows.

Honestly, the tool matters far less than the habit. A cheap tool you actually use every week beats a fancy one you never open.

sections.h2: What should you send, and how often, without annoying people?
sections.html:
This is where most restaurants go wrong. They finally build a list, get excited, and text it every day. Within a month half the list has tapped STOP. The fix is simple restraint.

How often

For most restaurants, two to four texts a month is the sweet spot. That is often enough to stay useful and rare enough that people are glad to hear from you. Over-texting is the number one reason people opt out, so when in doubt, send less. Watch your opt-out rate (your tool shows it). If it climbs much above one or two people per hundred on a send, you are texting too often or the offer is too weak.

When to send

For a slow-night fill, send in the late afternoon of that same day, roughly 3 to 5pm, when people are deciding what to do about dinner. A text at 4pm that says tonight only catches them at the exact moment of choice. Avoid early mornings and late nights. Nobody wants a taco ad at 7am.

What to send

Keep every text short (aim for one or two sentences), specific, and tied to a real reason to come in. A strong slow-night text has four parts: who it is from, the offer, the deadline, and the opt-out. For example: [Restaurant]: Tonight only, free flan with any 2 entrees, 5 to 9pm. Reply STOP to opt out. That is the whole recipe.

Two upgrades once you are comfortable. First, if your tool lets you segment (split your list into smaller groups), a separate list for happy-hour regulars or a bar crowd can handle a little more frequency. Second, in a Miami neighborhood with lots of Spanish-speaking guests, send the same offer in both English and Spanish. It takes 30 seconds and it reaches more of your block, for example: Solo hoy: postre gratis con 2 platos fuertes.

sections.h2: 5 texts you can copy for a slow night
sections.html:
Here are five texts you can adapt tonight. Swap in your restaurant name, your real offer, and your own number. Notice that every one is short, names a deadline, and ends with the opt-out. Keep each under about 160 characters so it sends as a single message.

  1. The straight deal: [Restaurant]: Tonight only, free dessert with any 2 entrees, 5 to 9pm. Walk in or call to reserve. Reply STOP to opt out.
  2. The themed night: It is Taco Tuesday at [Restaurant]! 3 tacos for 9 dollars all night, dine-in. See you tonight. Reply STOP to opt out.
  3. The slow-night rescue: [Restaurant]: Quiet night in the kitchen, loud deal for you. Free appetizer with any entree til 9pm tonight. Reply STOP to opt out.
  4. The family hook: [Restaurant]: Kids eat free with each adult meal tonight, 5 to 8pm. Bring the whole crew. Reply STOP to opt out.
  5. The regulars-only feel: [Restaurant]: You are on our list, so you get first dibs. Half-price bottles of wine tonight only. Reply STOP to opt out.

A few pointers. Lead with your restaurant name so people know instantly who is texting. Give one clear offer, not three. Always include the deadline (tonight, til 9pm), because urgency is what fills tonight's tables. And keep the opt-out on every single one. If you are near the beach or a hotel strip like Miami Beach during tourist season (roughly December through April), a line like walk-ins welcome helps visitors who did not plan ahead.

sections.h2: How do you tell if it is working?
sections.html:
You do not need a dashboard full of charts. Track one main number and two supporting ones.

The number that matters: covers on your slow night

Covers means guests served. Write down how many covers you do on your slow night, then send your text and compare the same night week over week. If your Tuesday covers climb over a few weeks of texting, the list is working. If they do not move, change the offer before you change anything else. A weak offer is the usual culprit, not the text itself.

Two supporting signals

  • Opt-out rate. Your tool shows how many people left after each send. A few is normal. A spike means you texted too often or the message missed. Keep it low and your list stays healthy for years.
  • Redemptions. If your offer uses a code or a simple mention this text line, count how many people cash it in. That tells you which offers actually pull people off the couch. Do more of the winners.

Give it a fair run. One text will not remake a Tuesday, but a steady list, messaged well twice a month, compounds. Three months in, that list becomes the first thing you reach for whenever the room is quiet.

faqs.q: What is restaurant SMS text message marketing?
faqs.a: Restaurant SMS text message marketing is sending short promotional texts to guests who gave you permission to contact them, usually to fill tables or push a special. SMS stands for Short Message Service, the plain text messages your phone already sends. Unlike social media, where an algorithm decides who sees your post, a text goes straight to the guest's phone and gets read within minutes almost every time. It works best for time-sensitive offers like a slow-night deal, because it reaches people right when they are deciding where to eat.

faqs.q: Do I need permission to text my restaurant customers?
faqs.a: Yes. Under the US TCPA law, you must get clear permission (an opt-in) before sending marketing texts, and every message must include an easy opt-out like Reply STOP. Permission means the guest actively agreed, by texting a keyword to join, checking a box they were not pre-checked into, or signing up under a notice that they will get texts. You cannot buy or scrape a list of numbers, and you cannot require the opt-in just to make a purchase. Only text people who invited you, and honor a STOP request right away.

faqs.q: How do I start collecting phone numbers for my restaurant?
faqs.a: Collect numbers at the moments guests are already happy, with permission built in. The easiest methods are a text-in keyword (text a word like TACOS to a number to join), table tents on every table, a quick ask at the checkout, a phone-number opt-in on your guest Wi-Fi login, and a QR code on receipts and takeout bags. Always show the honest small print, such as how many texts a month and Reply STOP to leave. Pick two methods and start this week. Your list grows one yes at a time.

faqs.q: How much does restaurant text message marketing cost?
faqs.a: For a small restaurant, expect roughly 25 to 50 dollars a month to start, though this is approximate and varies by tool. Plans are usually priced by how many texts you send, and an entry plan covering a few hundred to a couple thousand messages is plenty when you text only two to four times a month. If you already use Square, Toast, Clover, or SpotOn to ring up guests, texting may be built in or a low-cost add-on. Start with a small plan and only upgrade as your list grows.

faqs.q: How often should a restaurant text its customers?
faqs.a: Two to four texts a month is the sweet spot for most restaurants. That is frequent enough to stay useful and rare enough that guests are glad to hear from you. Over-texting is the top reason people opt out, so when in doubt, send less. Watch your opt-out rate after each send. If more than one or two people per hundred leave, you are either texting too often or your offer is too weak. Good timing and a real offer beat volume every time.

faqs.q: When is the best time to send a slow-night text?
faqs.a: Send in the late afternoon of the slow night itself, roughly 3 to 5pm, when people are deciding what to do about dinner. A text at 4pm that says tonight only reaches guests at the exact moment they are choosing where to eat, which is why same-day afternoon sends fill more tables than a morning or previous-day message. Avoid early mornings and late nights. Keep the message short, name a clear deadline, and always include the opt-out.

faqs.q: Is it legal to buy a list of phone numbers to text?
faqs.a: No. Buying, renting, or scraping phone numbers is against the TCPA and is the fastest way to get your number blocked and face fines that can run from hundreds to over a thousand dollars per message. People on a purchased list never agreed to hear from your restaurant, so texting them is both illegal and ineffective. The only list worth having is one you built yourself from guests who opted in. It is smaller at first, but it actually brings people through the door.

faqs.q: What should I do if a customer replies STOP?
faqs.a: Stop texting them immediately. When someone replies STOP, most texting tools remove that person from your list automatically, and you should never text them marketing again unless they choose to opt back in. Since 2025 you also must honor an opt-out made any reasonable way, so if a regular tells a server or emails you to stop the texts, take them off the list too. Respecting STOP keeps you compliant and protects your reputation with the guests who stay.
